M3_S01.summary: Sobhana means shining and radiant; the twenty-five beautiful mental factors are arranged in four groups, beginning with the nineteen beautiful universals.
body: Sobhana means shining, radiant, beautiful. The word carries both purity — clean, unmixed, untroubled — and goodness: wholesome, lovely, well made, skilful, right.
The group of beautiful mental factors comprises 25 cetasikas, arranged in four groups.
The first group is Sobhanasādhāraṇā, the beautiful universals, nineteen in number; they are present in every beautiful citta without exception.
The second group is Viratiyo, the abstinences, three in number: right speech (Sammāvācā), right action (Sammākammanto) and right livelihood (Sammā-ājīvo).

M3_S02.summary: The nineteen beautiful universals run from faith and mindfulness, through shame, dread, non-greed, non-hatred and equanimity, to the six body-mind pairs.
body: The list begins with seven single factors: 1. faith (Saddhā), 2. mindfulness (Sati), 3. moral shame (Hiri), 4. moral dread (Ottappa), 5. non-greed (Alobha), 6. non-hatred (Adosa), 7. equanimity or balance of mind (Tatramajjhattatā).
Then come the paired factors, the first pair being 8. tranquillity of mental factors (Kāyapassaddhi) and 9. tranquillity of consciousness (Cittapassaddhi).
Next: 10. lightness of mental factors (Kāyalahutā), 11. lightness of consciousness (Cittalahutā), 12. malleability of mental factors (Kāyamudutā), 13. malleability of consciousness (Cittamudutā).

Then: 14. wieldiness of mental factors (Kāyakammaññatā), 15. wieldiness of consciousness (Cittakammaññatā), 16. proficiency of mental factors (Kāyapāguññatā), 17. proficiency of consciousness (Cittapāguññatā).
Last: 18. rectitude of mental factors (Kāyujjukatā) and 19. rectitude of consciousness (Cittujjukatā).

Note the structure: numbers 8 to 19 are six twin pairs of body and mind (Kāya–Citta) — tranquillity, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, proficiency and rectitude, each in a factor-side and a consciousness-side form.

M3_S03.summary: Adding the two illimitables and the wisdom faculty to the nineteen universals and three abstinences gives the full twenty-five beautiful cetasikas.
body: The third group is Appamaññā, the illimitables, with two mental factors: compassion (Karuṇā) and appreciative joy (Muditā).
The fourth group is Paññindriya, the faculty of wisdom, a single mental factor.
Added together the four groups give the full count: 19 beautiful universals + 3 abstinences + 2 illimitables + 1 wisdom faculty = 25 beautiful mental factors.

One difference must be remembered: only the group of nineteen is 'universal', present in every beautiful citta. The other three groups — abstinences, illimitables and wisdom — arise only as the occasion requires.

M3_S04.summary: The three abstinences are the deliberate holding back from wrong speech, wrong action and wrong livelihood, and they arise only when the occasion for restraint appears.
body: Virati means abstinence, refraining, keeping away from. The group of abstinences (Viratiyo) has three mental factors: right speech (Sammāvācā), right action (Sammākammanto) and right livelihood (Sammā-ājīvo).

Right speech is abstinence in what is spoken: refraining from false speech (musāvāda), from divisive speech that sets people against one another (pisuṇāvācā), from harsh speech (pharusavācā) and from idle chatter (samphappalāpa).
Right action is rightful bodily conduct: abstaining from and cutting off the three bodily misdeeds — killing, stealing and sexual misconduct.
Right livelihood is earning one's living rightly: not using evil bodily or verbal action — killing, stealing, lying and the like — as a means of support.

Unlike the nineteen beautiful universals, these three arise only as the occasion demands and are not present in every beautiful citta: right speech, for instance, arises in a great wholesome citta at the moment one actually holds back from a lie.

M3_S05.summary: Faith, mindfulness, shame, dread, non-greed, non-hatred and equanimity head the group of nineteen: the cleansing, guarding and balancing factors of every wholesome mind.
body: Faith (Saddhā), from 'saṃ' (well, good) and 'dah' (to place, to set down), is confidence: placing the mind rightly upon its object, cleansing it and dispelling its uncertainty. Faith is of two kinds: wrong faith (micchāsaddhā), belief in what is not true — fanaticism and superstition — and right faith (sammāsaddhā), confidence in what truly is: in kamma, in its results, and in the enlightenment of the Blessed One.

Mindfulness (Sati), from the root 'sar' (to remember, to recall), has as its real state the absence of forgetting: it guards against the arising of evil states and keeps wholesome states arising without interruption, noting and remaining aware of body, feelings, mind and mental objects.

Moral shame (Hiri) is the reluctance, the hesitancy, the sense of disgrace felt at the evil and faulty deeds that might issue from body or speech. Five things make shame arise: noble birth, maturity of age, social standing, education, and the Buddha's teaching.

Moral dread (Ottappa) is fear and horror — the mind trembles at the danger seen in evil bodily and verbal action. Four things make dread arise: fear of punishment, fear of painful destinies, fear of being blamed, and fear of one's own conscience.

Shame and dread are twins: they are called the two bright states and the two guardians of the world, since they keep body and mind from transgression, and they are the states that make a true recluse. Shame is the opposite of shamelessness and dread the opposite of fearlessness of wrongdoing, both studied in module M2.

Non-greed (Alobha) is non-attachment, like water rolling off a lotus leaf: it meets the object without sticking to it. It shows itself as generosity, giving and altruism — letting go, relinquishing, not clinging, not appropriating — and it is the direct opposite of selfishness and infatuation. It is one of the three wholesome roots.

Non-hatred (Adosa) is freedom from resentment, anger, indignation and irritation when facing what is disagreeable: patience and composure in adverse circumstances, coolness, loving-kindness. Its mark is harmlessness, absence of malice, absence of opposition. It too is one of the three wholesome roots.

Equanimity (Tatramajjhattatā) — 'tatra' (there, in that) and 'majjhattatā' (standing in the middle) — leans to neither side, but keeps the balance. Its mark is impartiality, and it keeps the mental states arisen with it in even measure. Developed to its height it becomes the illimitable of equanimity, the deliverance of mind through equanimity, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

M3_S06.summary: In the six pairs, 'body' means the group of mental factors and 'mind' means consciousness itself; together they cure agitation, heaviness, rigidity, unwieldiness, weakness and crookedness.
body: The meaning of the pairing: 'body' (Kāya) here denotes the group of mental factors — the aggregates of feeling, perception and formations; 'mind' (Citta) denotes the aggregate of consciousness, that is, the citta itself. Thus Kāyapassaddhi is the factor that calms the other mental factors (not the physical body), while Cittapassaddhi is the factor that calms consciousness.

Tranquillity of factors and of consciousness (Kāyapassaddhi – Cittapassaddhi, nos. 8–9): passaddhi is stillness, quiet, ease. It soothes agitation so that consciousness and its factors no longer waver, and it cools the fever of desire. This pair is the antidote to restlessness.

Lightness of factors and of consciousness (Kāyalahutā – Cittalahutā, nos. 10–11): from 'laghu', light and quick. It is buoyancy, the shedding of the heaviness of the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, and it is the opposite of sloth and torpor, which make mind and factors heavy and sluggish.

Malleability of factors and of consciousness (Kāyamudutā – Cittamudutā, nos. 12–13): 'mudu' means soft, gentle, easily shaped. It is pliancy without coarseness or stubbornness, dissolving the rigidity of mind and factors. What makes the mind rigid: wrong view, conceit, doubt about the Triple Gem, and angry opposition to fellow practitioners.

Wieldiness of factors and of consciousness (Kāyakammaññatā – Cittakammaññatā, nos. 14–15): 'kamma + ñña + tā', the state of being workable, fit for the task. It dissolves unfitness in mind and factors, and is the opposite of sensual desire, ill will and doubt. With this pair, wholesome practice comes easily and the jhānas and higher knowledges are readily attained.

Proficiency of factors and of consciousness (Kāyapāguññatā – Cittapāguññatā, nos. 16–17): 'pa + guṇ + tā', skill and polish through practice. It removes the sickly, feeble, sluggish condition of mind and factors, and is the opposite of lack of faith and lack of confidence.

Rectitude of factors and of consciousness (Kāyujjukatā – Cittujjukatā, nos. 18–19): 'uju' means straight; ujukatā is uprightness, honesty, absence of bends and crookedness. Rectitude of factors is the straightness of the aggregates of feeling, perception and formations (the remaining mental factors); rectitude of consciousness is the straightness of the aggregate of consciousness, the citta.

To conclude on the group of nineteen: these nineteen beautiful factors arise together with every beautiful citta, and for that reason are called the beautiful universals. The remaining six of the twenty-five arise only at particular times, in particular cittas.

M3_S07.summary: Compassion wishes beings free from suffering and appreciative joy rejoices in their good fortune, while the faculty of wisdom penetrates things as they really are.
body: Appamaññā means immeasurable, without limit: the object of these two mental factors is the boundless field of living beings, taken without discrimination and without restriction to any class of being.

Compassion (Karuṇā), from 'kar' with 'uṇa', is the tender heart that trembles at the sight of another's suffering. Its characteristic is the wish that beings be free from suffering; its function is the inability to bear the sight of their pain. Its near enemy is cruelty and rage; its indirect enemy is the grief that arises when one cannot help a suffering being.

Compassion usually arises with neutral feeling, since its object is a being in distress — without wise attention, displeasure arises instead and the mind becomes hatred-rooted. Compassion is accompanied by joy only when one sees a being released from the suffering that tormented it.

Appreciative joy (Muditā), from the root 'mud' (to be glad, to be content), is gladness at the beauty, the goodness and the happiness of others; its function is not to envy other beings. Its near enemy is jealousy.

Compassion and appreciative joy are two of the four illimitables (loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, equanimity). As the teaching concludes, loving-kindness is in fact the factor of non-hatred, and the fourth illimitable is the factor of equanimity (Tatramajjhattatā).

The faculty of wisdom (Paññindriya): 'pa' means fully, completely, rightly; 'ñā' means knowing — paññā is therefore complete and correct knowing. Indriya means faculty: a controlling power within its own domain, as in the five faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration and wisdom.
The mark of wisdom is penetrative understanding: it sees through to the real nature of phenomena just as they are. As far as wisdom reaches, so far does ignorance dissolve.

Wisdom is threefold: wisdom from learning (suttamayā paññā), arising from listening to and gathering the Dhamma taught by others; wisdom from reflection (cintāmayā paññā), arising from one's own thinking and analysis; and wisdom from development (bhāvanāmayā paññā), arising from practice, direct experience and meditation.

M5_S01.summary: The 24 sense-sphere beautiful cittas fall into three sets of eight: great wholesome (the cause), great resultant (the result) and great functional (the Arahant's conduct).
body: Kāmāvacara means frequenting the sense sphere: these are the lovely cittas that regularly occur and move about in the sensuous realm. Sobhaṇa means beautiful, good, radiant.
The sense-sphere beautiful cittas are of three kinds, 24 in all: 8 great wholesome cittas (Mahākusala), 8 great resultant cittas (Mahāvipāka) and 8 great functional cittas (Mahākiriya).

The great wholesome cittas are the good causes that will bring good results — the causes that bring about birth as a human being or a sense-sphere deity. They are called 'great' because with them a vast amount of merit can be made, the ten bases of meritorious action.
The great resultant cittas are the matured results of those wholesome causes.
The great functional cittas belong to the Arahants: since they no longer create causes, functional consciousness takes the place that great wholesome consciousness occupies in others.

M5_S02.summary: The eight great wholesome cittas are formed by crossing feeling (joy or equanimity), knowledge (present or absent) and prompting (absent or present): 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
body: The eight great wholesome cittas are distinguished by three contrasting pairs: joy (somanassa) or equanimity (upekkhā); associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta) or dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta); unprompted (asaṅkhārika) or prompted (sasaṅkhārika).
The first is named in full: 'Somanassa-sahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ ekaṃ' — a great wholesome citta accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, unprompted.
The second: joy, with knowledge, prompted. The third: joy, without knowledge, unprompted. The fourth: joy, without knowledge, prompted.

The fifth: equanimity, with knowledge, unprompted. The sixth: equanimity, with knowledge, prompted. The seventh: equanimity, without knowledge, unprompted. The eighth: equanimity, without knowledge, prompted.

The key difference from the eight greed-rooted cittas: those are divided by wrong view (associated or dissociated), whereas the great wholesome cittas are divided by knowledge (associated or dissociated).

M5_S03.summary: Sense-sphere beautiful cittas arise in beings of every kind and in all realms where they can occur — only the Arahant replaces the wholesome ones with functional cittas.
body: With the great wholesome cittas the ten bases of meritorious action are performed: giving, virtue, meditation, reverence, service, sharing merit, rejoicing in merit, listening to the Dhamma, teaching the Dhamma, and straightening one's view.
These cittas arise in many kinds of being: in ghosts, animals and hell beings, in human beings, in deities and brahmās, and in the noble disciples still in training.
The one exception is the Arahant: having nothing more to accomplish, the Arahant uses great functional cittas in place of great wholesome cittas.
Although they are called kāmāvacara, these cittas also occur in the form and formless realms — but not as constantly as they do in the sense sphere, which is their proper home.
